# Agent time cutoffs

<!-- Generated from scripts/task_cutoffs.toml by `python3 scripts/task_cutoffs.py apply`. Do not edit this file: edit the table and run the command. -->

Every task gives the agent a fixed wall-clock time, its **cutoff**: Harbor's `[agent] timeout_sec`. At the cutoff the agent is stopped and the trial is graded as it stands ([PROTOCOL.md](PROTOCOL.md) §2.12). The numbers live in one file, [`scripts/task_cutoffs.toml`](../scripts/task_cutoffs.toml): seconds per benchmark and mode, with optional exceptions per family and per task. This page shows that table and is rendered from it.

**When the clock starts.** Harbor counts the cutoff around the agent's run only (`asyncio.wait_for(agent.run(...), timeout=...)` in its trial's agent phase): after the environment has been built and started and after the agent's harness has been installed, each of which has a timeout of its own. It does not count from the container's start. In the standard modes the `sim` service starts with the environment, so whatever start-up it has not finished by then is waited out inside the agent's time.

## Exceptions (per family, per task)

A benchmark's row is the default of all its tasks in a mode. The table may give one family, or one task, another number; the most specific entry wins: **task > family > benchmark and mode**. A family is `[metadata] family` in `task.toml` (`python3 scripts/task_cutoffs.py families "<benchmark>"` lists a benchmark's). Like every cutoff, an exception is an owner decision with a `[[history]]` entry, and results are compared only under the same cutoff (PROTOCOL D8).

```toml
[family_cutoff_sec."RoboARC"]              # benchmark; then one line per family, a number per mode
"cast_coil" = { privileged = 14400, standard = 14400 }

[task_cutoff_sec]                              # one line per task directory
"roboarc-cast-coil-05-i01-standard" = 10800
```

No exception is in use: every task takes its benchmark's number.

## What the agent is told

Every `instruction.md` ends with the same section, written by `scripts/task_conventions.py` from the table: the last thing the agent reads (here for 3600 s; the first paragraph is the same in every mode):

> ## Time limit
> You have 3600 seconds to complete this task. Do not cheat by using online solutions or hints specific to this task.
>
> This is wall-clock time from the start of your session; the time a simulator takes to start counts. When it is up you are stopped without warning and only what is in `/app/output/` at that moment is graded, so save a deliverable as soon as you have one and overwrite it whenever you have a better one. Your session started when you received this task: run `date` now, and again before you decide that time is short; work out the time left from those readings, never from a guess. Installing packages is not cheating (`## External material` above).

In the standard and standard-realtime modes the second paragraph is:

> This is wall-clock time from the start of your session; the time you wait for the simulator service counts. When it is up you are stopped without warning and the episode is graded as it stands at that moment. The service's `time_left_s` counts the same limit from your first request to the service, so it never runs out before your time does: your real time left is `time_left_s` minus the time you spent before that request. Plan by it. Your session started when you received this task: run `date` now, and again before you decide that time is short; work out the time left from those readings, never from a guess. Installing packages is not cheating (`## External material` above).

(No benchmark keeps the earlier, weaker sentence today: every service counts from the agent's first request.)

What a benchmark adds about its own time (a simulator's start-up, what its service counts) stands in its own text and names no number: it says "the time limit (`## Time limit`)".

## Changing a cutoff

1. Edit the number in [`scripts/task_cutoffs.toml`](../scripts/task_cutoffs.toml) (the benchmark's row, or an exception) and add a `[[history]]` entry at its end (date, who decided, from -> to, why). It is required: CI and `apply` refuse a number that differs from its last recorded value.
2. `python3 scripts/task_cutoffs.py apply` (about three minutes; `apply "<benchmark>"` for one benchmark).
3. Commit everything it changed and open a pull request. CI (`ci_checks/check-cutoffs.py`) fails when a task's `task.toml`, its instruction or its sim service disagrees with the table.

Never edit the number in a task, a template or a generator. `apply` writes, in every task concerned: `[agent] timeout_sec`, the number in the closing section of `instruction.md`, the README's `Agent time budget` row, the sim service's `RCB_WALL_CLOCK_S` (standard modes), the task's digest in `tasks/dataset.toml`, and this page.

A change of a cutoff changes the task in place: the scene, the frozen instance, the success rule and the verifier are the same, so the task keeps its name (PROTOCOL §2.8, §2.12). The record of the change is its `[[history]]` entry (below), not a Change Log entry in each task's README. A number's last recorded value is its newest entry's, or, if it never changed, the table of 2026-10-11 ([`scripts/task_cutoffs.baseline.toml`](../scripts/task_cutoffs.baseline.toml), never edited). Results recorded under another cutoff are reported separately (PROTOCOL D8), and trials already running keep the cutoff they started with.

## What follows the number, and what does not

- **Follows by itself** (`apply`): everything listed above, and a scheduler's estimate of a trial's length, which reads `task.toml`.
- **The sim service's clock** (`RCB_WALL_CLOCK_S`) only reports: `spec["budget"]["wall_clock_s"]` and `meta["time_left_s"]`, counted from the agent's first request to the service (any endpoint; kept through a restart of the service), never from the service's start: the service is up before the agent's phase begins, so a clock started with it ran ahead of Harbor's (a median of 79 s over the recorded trials). Harbor's timeout is what stops the agent. RoboARC's service still ends the episode itself when its own count reaches 0; since its MuJoCo release (2026-10-13) that count starts at the first request, so it is never before Harbor's timeout (to become report-only at RoboARC's next task update: `docs/benchmarks/roboarc.md`).
- **Look at these when you raise a cutoff** (lowering one is safe): the collect-hook and verifier budgets that were sized for an episode as long as the agent's time (RoboCasa, RoboCasa365 and RoboCasa-GR1 `COLLECT_TIMEOUT_S`; RoboLab, YAMLab, DexJoCo and BEHAVIOR-1K, see their `docs/benchmarks/` pages), and the cap of 14400 s.
- **RoboOlympics**: the cutoff has to stay above a match's wall time (5 to 60 minutes at slowdown 10).
- **Not derived from it**: the token budget (PROTOCOL §5), the resource limits (§2.10), reset budgets, step caps, verifier timeouts.
